claims.text: Post-synthesis thermal annealing creates a more homogeneous microstructure in the selected high-entropy alloy.
Annealing-induced microstructural homogeneity enhances electron-phonon coupling.
The enhancement of electron-phonon coupling caused by annealing is sufficient to trigger low-temperature superconductivity.
The unannealed as-cast state does not exhibit coherent superconductivity.
The as-cast alloy has relatively high compositional and microstructural disorder.
Annealing increases microstructural homogeneity and reduces lattice and chemical disorder.
Reduced lattice and chemical disorder improves the electron-phonon interaction network.
Annealing reduces internal strains and local compositional fluctuations.
Reduced internal strain and compositional fluctuations produce a more coherent lattice.
Improved structural order enables stronger and more spatially uniform electron-phonon coupling.
Stronger and more uniform electron-phonon coupling enables superconductivity below a critical temperature.
Excessive disorder in the unannealed state suppresses formation of a coherent superconducting phase.
Relative to the as-cast control, the annealed alloy will develop a superconducting transition characterized by a sharp resistivity drop to zero.
The proposed effect requires enough annealing to produce appreciable homogenization without creating unwanted secondary phases.
Annealing conditions that cause phase separation or excessive grain growth may prevent the proposed superconductivity enhancement.
The superconducting transition temperature and required degree of homogenization depend on alloy composition and annealing parameters.
